articleTitle: An experimental application of microprocessors to railway signalling
abstract: The Research & Development Division of British Rail is engaged in a programme of development which, it is hoped, will result in a microprocessor-based alternative to the electromechanical interlocking equipment used in present-day signalling systems. An alternative system must match the outstanding safety and reliability of present-day signalling technology, which has evolved over a long period of time

articleTitle: Treeing in solid extruded electrical insulation
abstract: Over 90% of failures in buried cables are caused by mechanical damage, and, of the remaining 10%, the cause is unknown. Trees have been found in the polyethylene insulation of cables that have failed in service, but nobody has established that treeing was the actual cause of failure. But, because of the increasingly severe requirements for power systems, all factors must be considered to design for complete reliability

articleTitle: Partial removal of transmission errors in digitally encoded speech
abstract: Error protection coding is often used to combat the effect of transmission errors in binary encoded speech, but, if data throughput is to be kept constant, it requires an increase in transmission bit rate. An alternative approach, which does not use a protection code, decodes the erroneous speech at the receiver, inspects it, deduces the effect of transmission errors, and partially corrects it using a simple statistical hypothesis

articleTitle: Protection of data processing equipment against static electricity discharges
abstract: The fact that electric charges can be produced by friction has been known for several thousandyears, and for most of that time people have been aware of the danger of fires being caused by sparks generated in this way. During the last decade the combination of synthetic fabrics and the dryatmospheres produced by central heating has made discharges of this sort common, and the fast logic circuits used in modem data-processing equipment have often proved susceptible to interference

articleTitle: Application of thyristor inverters in induction heating and melting
abstract: The use of static power supplies using solid-state devices in the induction-heating industry has increased greatly over the past years. This article reviews the principles involved in the design of thyristor-controlled inverters in the induction-heating and melting industry

articleTitle: Electronics in the control of turbine generators
abstract: From its invention at the end of the last century, up to the period of the late 1950s, steam-turbine plant was an uncompromising area of mechanical engineering; electrical devices generally only appeared in the form of thermocouples for temperature measurement, and relatively little progress had been made, or indeed thought given, to the possibility of applying the newer disciplines of electronics and control engineering. But today sophisiticated electrohydraulic governors are almost universal for larger new plant; turbine instrumentation has become more accurate and reliable; and digital techniques are already in use and seem set to gain ground in the future.

The utilisation of electrical energy in an advanced technological society is closely related to the quality of life. The general acceptance and utilisation of reliability-engineering concepts in all phases of utility management, design and operation is vital if the electric power industry is to continue to satisfy the system-load requirement as economically as possible and with a reasonable assurance of continuity and quality

articleTitle: Electrical induction heating for the processing of fossil fuels
abstract: The fossil fuels are nonmagnetic partial conductors of electricity with relatively high electromagnetic loss factors. They also absorb energy efficiently from an alternating electromagnetic field, these characteristics are ideal for in situ electrical induction heating, which permits environmentally clean production of petroleum, natural gas, coal tar and electricity on large scales

Stepping rates as high as 20 000 steps/second are now not unusual in stepping-motor systems. To achieve such high rates, the drive circuits must be more sophisticated than for single stepping, and many different techniques are in use. By using these techniques, even relatively poor motors, most of them designed as static devices, can be forced to run fast by providing sufficient power in the drive circuits. The need for this `sledgehammer' approach can, however, be reduced if both the motor and its drive are designed specifically for high-speed running

articleTitle: Power transistors in variable speed drives
abstract: Since the mid-1960s, thyristors have become established as the power control element in applications from domestic lighting and washing-machine controllers to d.c. rolling-mill drives and inverters for alternator starting, with ratings up to at least 10 MW. During this period, transistors were also evolving into types suitable for power control. Today, British-developed 500 V 300 A transistors are being applied to d.c. servo drives and inverters for multiple-unit traction drives. In application to both a.c.- and d.c.-motor drives, the fast switching capability of transistors can have advantages over thyristors, and we shall see it grow as an alternative power controller

articleTitle: Frequency measurements by frequency meter or timer counter?
abstract: Throughout industry there are numerous requirements for the measurement of frequency in the range 0.001 Hz to 10 MHz. These application areas include servomechanisms, electromechanical systems, industrial instrumentation, medical instrumentation, power systems, telephony, audio systems, radio down to the 30 m waveband, television video circuits and digital systems. However, to meet these requirements, the user has a choice in type of instrument between a frequency meter and a timer counter. Recent developments in frequency meters make the comparison worthy of even greater investigation

Have you ever dreamed of owning a wonder car, with touch buttons for everything, including the gear shift? Well £32 620 will buy you the Aston Martin Lagonda, which boasts two microprocessors and a total of about 48 touch buttons for you to play with while you are stuck in a London traffic jam

articleTitle: Technical alternatives for a maglev system
abstract: The research effort of the last six years in W. Germany has reduced the alternatives for the lift, guidance and propulsion of a magnetically levitated train with maximum speeds of from 400 to 500 km/h to essentially two possibilities with one additional variant: the electromagnetic levitation system (e.m.s.) being developed by the consortium Transrapid-EMS (Krauss-Maffei & MBB) together with Thyssen Henschel and Universitied, and, secondly, the electrodynamic levitation system (e.d.s.) of the project group AEG-BBC-Siemens.

articleTitle: Improve project leadership with the aid of a communication infrastructure
abstract: Within the framework of an engineering design project, great emphasis is placed on the availability of modern technical resources and talented personnel However project organisation, monitoring and reporting, together with the psychological requirements of project management, are all too often overlooked to the detriment of the final product

One of the most common problems with large software packages is that they tend to be badly documented. With hardware products we expect a wide range of documentation from functional descriptions of the equipment to maintenance handbooks and circuit diagrams. Software products have similar needs, but these are rarely satisfied, so that maintenance teams may find themselves trying to support packages which they cannot even understand, let alone maintain

We are witnessing an inexorable growth in the electronic handling of information, and optical-fibre communication systems will make a large contribution to this growth. But just where will optical communication systems make their impact in society given their present physical limitations and performance?

articleTitle: Try harder and get that job
abstract: The aim of this article is to assist anyone who is seeking a new job. Everyone concerned with the recruitment of staff can tell of the poor quality of many applications received. Lack of vital information and poor presentation can lead to a candidate not being offered an interview. The answer to this situation lies in the hands of the applicant. More thought and effort at the application stage greatly increases the chance of being offered an interview and, ultimately, a job

articleTitle: Computer fraud. The villain's view of the opportunities
abstract: Are you sure that your computer system is safe from villains? Remember, most villains have to be very unlucky to get caught. Are you still sure you have full security? Well, you may not be so sure when you get to the end of this article.

articleTitle: Electrical engineering and the European Community
abstract: There is no doubt that the European Economic Community is today Britain's biggest expanding market for export. Between 1970 and 1972 when Britain was outside the EEC it had been sharply declining. By contrast, British exports to the EEC have risen by 87% in real terms between 1972 and the first quarter of 1977. On the other hand, British exports to the rest of the world rose only 49% in real terms in the same period. If the EEC had remained the `rest of the world' and grown at the same rate of around 49%, Britain would now be losing export worth over some £2.2 billion a year. That has meant an immense saving in British jobs, probably around 450 000 altogether. There is therefore a major national incentive for everyone in British industry to `think European' in the years that lie ahead

articleTitle: Developing new technologies - how Britain can beat the rest
abstract: DR. CYRIL HILSUM, the only chief scientific officer of the Ministry of Defence appointed to a research position, found himself just after the Second World War working for the Admiralty rather than staying on at University College, London, as its Physics Department's first post-war postgraduate research student. He was sent to join Admiralty headquarters, and after working on the British infrared programme, moved on to compound semiconductors. He was one of the scientists involved in investigating gallium arsenide's instabilities, although it was Gunn who named the oscillation effect and the resulting diode. He now researches with The Royal Signals & Radar Establishment on solid-state flat-panel displays, and holds the highest scientific-officer grade the UK Civil Service can offer without administrative responsibilities. CAROLINE WEINSTEIN went to see him recently to talk about a little of his career and his views on science and technological research in the UK.

articleTitle: Distributed computer control for power station plant
abstract: This article gives one approach to the implementation of distributed hierarchical control systems for a 120 MW coal-fired boiler at Skelton Grange Power Station. The essential feature has been to determine the functional needs of the hierarchy and define a common software system for the whole hierarchy, but with selectable subsets for inclusion at different levels optimised to their function, as well as handling the inter-processor communication requirements.

The rate of progress in design concepts of computer hardware has accelerated rapidly over the last ten years, helped by the semiconductor industry. Integrated-circuit technology is still advancing with great speed, permitting faster and smaller mainframes to be made

articleTitle: Balzers High Vacuum keeps up the pressure
The Windscale Inquiry. Dennis Moralee comments on Mr. Justice Parker's conclusions
abstract: At the outset of the Inquiry I posed three questions which appeared to me to be sufficient to cover all issues which had then been indicated. These questions were: 1. Should oxide fuel from United Kingdom reactors be reprocessed in this country at all, whether at Windscale or elsewhere? 2. If yes, should such reprocessing be carried on at Windscale? 3. If yes, should the reprocessing plant be about double the estimated size required to handle United Kingdom oxide fuels and be used, as to the spare capacity, for reprocessing foreign fuels? These three questions still appear to me to cover all the issues raised at the Inquiry, numerous as they were Mr. Justice Parker, Windscale Report

articleTitle: Floppy discs. The storage medium for microprocessor systems
abstract: The rapid growth of the market for small microprocessor-based systems has made the floppy-disc drive, which provides mass storage at a price/performance level ideally suited to these systems, probably the most widely used system component of all time. As the performance of a system's mass storage devices can determine its overall performance, detailed knowledge of the floppy-disc drive's operating characteristics is essential for all those engaged in the design of microprocessor-based systems

articleTitle: Finance for industry. Part 3: Capital markets overseas
abstract: In the previous two articles in the series, which were published in E&P in July and August 1978, we looked at the options open to both the private and public company in the UK seeking finance for expansion. In this article, we are making a foray overseas to examine the relationship between businessmen and bankers in the USA and in Western Europe, and how their `financial-engineering' systems differ from that of the UK. Before so doing, it is essential briefly to comment on the world's only international capital market-usually known as the `Eurodollar market'

The spectrum analyser, once a laboratory curiosity, is now one of the most powerful tools available to the electronics industry. The advent of microprocessor control and digital storage has increased the versatility of spectrum analysers, and new circuit techniques are extending their applications into the microwave region

When broadcasting began in Britain, in 1922, the Government of the day decided to place the tasks of creating programmes, providing the engineering services and operating the transmitters in the hands of a single organisation. In broadcast engineering, the BBC set very high professional standards and still maintains a leading position for innovation and quality

articleTitle: Solid-state serial memories. The role of bubbles and c.c.d.s.
abstract: Solid-state memories are rapidly becoming the dominant medium for information storage in digital systems. Their ascendance has been steady, almost slow, until recently. The situation has changed dramatically during the last few years because of technology and circuit advances offering substantial benefits to the user in terms of cost, versatility and performance.

articleTitle: Prof. Sir Hermann Bondi: a man of energy
abstract: A varied and distinguished career has preceded Prof. Sir Hermann Bondi's appointment to the post of Chief Scientist at the UK Department of Energy. He met Caroline Weinstein recently and discussed Britain's current and future needs for energy and various other resources.

articleTitle: Electric Power Research Institute. A power 'think tank' in Silicon Valley
abstract: In the heart of Silicon Valley in California, amid the numerous electronics companies, is an organisation developing and administering a co-ordinated national electrical power r. & d. programme. Tony Prins visited the Electric Power Research Institute in Palo Alto in California recently and discussed a handful of EPRI's 750 or so projects with John Dougherty, Director, Electrical Systems Division.

If any technological advance can be acclaimed as a miracle, the large-scale integration (l.s.i.) of electronic components certainly can. Microminiaturisation and consequent low costs have revolutionised electronic design, and a major achievement has been the processor-on-the-chip: the microprocessor, which, combined with other l.s.i. components like memory and input/output, forms a microcomputer. Being so much smaller and cheaper than existing minicomputers, they have already had a significant impact, and it is inevitable that they will be introduced to advantage in many new fields. But there is a grave danger that the very idea of microcomputers is being `oversold' before the full costs and supporting technologies are established. Publicity can too easily gloss over implementation costs, e.g. program-development facilities and prototyping hardware. Design engineers must investigate some of these hidden costs, and identify the support software required if microcomputers are to fulfil their promise

articleTitle: Solid-state devices and the age of indolence
abstract: Solid-state device technology is extending man's capabilities and the subsequent change in manufacturing technology offers a major threat to large segments of existing manufacturing industry, although, simultaneously, the same technology is creating major new markets - many indeed associated with the growing leisure industries. Hence the overall relationship between solid-state device technology and indolence in its widest sense would seem to be: first, current trends in silicon integrated-circuit technology lead inexorably to the need for massive redeployment and retraining of people currently employed in many existing industries; secondly, this same technology is creating many new market and job opportunities, frequently associated with the consumer and leisure industries; and, thirdly, a useful way of forecasting further technical change is to work on the assumption that it will be in such a direction as to make life `easier' for the manufacturer or the user - or both

The `Carabian conundrum' is a fictitious case study based on a live automation contract. Each chapter will concern itself with a particular phase of project management. In particular, the firm's response to different situations will be described. In the first chapter, printed in July, you were introduced to Iloma Systems Ltd., a small `projects' company within the giant Thanrico International. Through Iloma's agent in Carabia, a small South American state, it had entered into preliminary discussions about the possibility of tendering for a radar automation contract about to be let by the country's nationalised communication company, CITE. Rough estimates had indicated that the job would be worth £4 million and take two years to complete. After considering the problems involved the Board had instructed the Projects Director to proceed with preparing a detailed strategy document describing the methods to be adopted to reduce the inherent risks. We are asking you to be involved-to analyse the situation and propose action which you believe the firm should have taken based on your experience. A selection of responses will be printed in a future edition. If you feel you have something to offer, please respond to David Overton at the address shown below.

articleTitle: Microprocessor analysers in the development and support of microprocessor-based systems
abstract: When designers working with logic circuits found that the available equipment, primarily multichannel oscilloscopes, was severely limited in their ability to help them solve problems, a new instrument was introduced to help - the logic analyser. It appeared in two forms: the logic-state analyser and the logic-timing analyser

This article is about problem solving: a process that involves gathering information, speculation about possible solutions and finally the choice of a `best' answer. As a solution emerges, it may uncover a new aspect of the problem that demands attention. This tends to make the process an iterative one

It may seem to many a businessman, building up a company, that banks are solely concerned with the figures which appear on that company's balance sheet at the end of the year - figures which, while providing a useful gauge to measure a company's progress, are only a snapshot of the company's financial position at one moment in time. As the following article shows, bankers are not just interested in company balance sheets. They need to understand the conditions in which the company operates, the problems it faces, the quality of the management to weather both fair winds and foul, and, most important of all, to translate the management's ambitions for their companies into reality by designing the appropriate financial facilities - `financial engineering' is no bad description for the role of many bankers today. To bring the interrelationship of business and banker together, this article has been written in the form of a case history. While it is hypothetical - in order to encompass as many of a company's banking relationships as possible over a period of years - it is based on an amalgam of real-life situations

articleTitle: Power consumption for alternative maglev systems
abstract: Two alternative systems for a high speed train are being developed in W. Germany, namely, the electrodynamic system of levitation utilising superconducting magnets and the long-stator synchronous motor for propulsion e. d. s.), and the electromagnetic attraction system of suspension using controlled electromagnets combined with either the short-stator linear induction motor or the long-stator synchronous motor for propulsion e. m. s.).

articleTitle: Spy satellites. Somebody could be watching you
abstract: Next time you look up into a cloudless blue sky, it is worth remembering that someone up there might be watching you. Should you be anywhere near a military installation, like an airfield or missile base, you could be within the field of view of an orbiting spy in the sky, a satellite carrying cameras so powereful as to be capable of detecting that you are a mere civilian and not a guard or sentry in uniform. Space research and manned missions may grab the headlines, but military satellites grab the budget, outnumbering their more glamorous counterparts by three to one

articleTitle: Will microcomputers be a boon for Britain?
abstract: ALEX D'AGAPEYEFF is founder and chairman of one of Britain's biggest software houses and an advocate of the microcomputer and its possibilities. He warns that Britain is in danger of losing an enormous amount of business if it does not quickly begin making products designed around microcomputers. He talks to CAROLINE WEINSTEIN

articleTitle: A few years ago the product was king, today we are selling service
abstract: The telecommunication industry has been under a cloud in recent years as the British Post Office cut back its orders. Consequently, its equipment suppliers have been forced to trim their workforces, and Standard Telephones & Cables Ltd. has been no exception. CAROLINE WEINSTEIN asked KENNETH CORFIELD, deputy chairman and managing director of STC, how he saw the future

articleTitle: Practical considerations of laser doppler anemometry
abstract: The laser doppler anemometer is a comparatively new tool for flow measurements. This article outlines the principles behind `dual-beam' laser anemometry using the fringe model and relates the role of l.d.a. in fluid dynamics research. The techniques are illustrated with reference to systems available at University College, Cardiff

When one considers the defence of one's country, it may be fashionable to think first of air defence and therefore of aircraft. However, the ship is also a fighting platform from which to attack and destroy enemy targets in the air and the Royal Navy is modernising its fleet and equipping it with newer missiles

articleTitle: A reading aid for the partially sighted
abstract: There are several reading aids to help the partially sighted, the more sophisticated of which employ closed-circuit television. However, this latter type is very expensive and generally non-portable. A new reading aid has been devised by engineers at Philips Research Laboratories which retains most of the c.c.t.v. system advantages while at the same time being portable and costing less

The East Anglian Regional Health Authority has under construction at the St. John's hospital site at Peterborough a 140-bed building project for geriatric patients, which will become Britain's first all-electric hospital. Clearly, all hospital buildings are using electricity as an energy source for a wide variety of applications. The term `all-electric' is an easy colloquial way of describing a hospital that depends exclusively on electricity as an energy source for all purposes, including space heating, domestic hot water supply and for meal preparation and cooking

articleTitle: The research engineer and the screw
abstract: An empirical law of innovation may be stated as: `All engineers tend to innovate unless prevented by a superior force'. This applies over virtually the whole range of engineering activities, from exploratory research to the operation and maintenance of established equipment. In the training of engineers, the problem is not so much to attempt to teach engineers to innovate. They will do that anyway. Rather the problem is to train them in developing and guiding their innovative instincts to best further the interests of the organisation and the community at large

The problem of how to control industrial research for the benefit of the company or society which supports it is a subject of perennial interest. Ever since science based industry became a recognised component of society, those concerned with the deployment of resources on industrial research have been uneasily aware that there is very little correlation between expenditure and recognisably useful results. This article tackles the problem by the analysis of observations on the practice and exploitation of industrial research

articleTitle: The Cardiff urban traffic control scheme
abstract: South Glamorgan County Council is installing a computer-based urban traffic control system in the Cardiff area, but it is not considered to be a panacea or the complete solution to Cardiff's traffic problems. However, it should ensure that the road network is used effectively and efficiently when the system is commissioned this year

articleTitle: Introducing the new Great Northern Electric service
abstract: The Great Northern Suburban Electrification, authorised in 1971, became a reality in 1978 with the introduction of Class 312 electric multiple units on Outer Suburban Services from Royston to London, Kings Cross. This event followed 15 months after the changeover from diesel to electric on the Inner Suburban Services operated from Welwyn Garden City and Hertford to Moorgate, London, by Class 313 electric multiple units since November 1976. From its inception to completion has taken 6 years and fulfils electrification proposals first conceived by the Great Northern Railway Company in 1903

articleTitle: The electric way ahead for road transport
abstract: In the latter part of this century and the early decades of the next, there will be widespread use of electric road vehicles. This is the opinion of the Electric Vehicle Development Group. But what do the EVDG think are the factors that will influence changes in this direction?

articleTitle: Industrial democracy ߝ which way is best for Britain?
abstract: You can take your pick of the many ideas on how best to have a good working relationship between management and the shop floor - there are as many methods as there are managers. The British Government recently published a White Paper on industrial democracy that contained its thoughts on the matter, but many companies believe they have found the key already

Many of the earliest dynamo-electric machines had permanent-magnet excitation. Gradually, however, this form of excitation was replaced by excitation from electromagnets, which seemed to offer the advantage of stronger magnetic fields and so more power from a total volume of material. Since then, many signs have appeared that indicate a reversal of this trend. Small permanent-magnet direct-current motors are commonplace in automobiles. Perhaps most interestingly, new forms of alternating-current machine using permanent magnets have begun to appear, and these show some interesting advantages compared with alternative drive systems. The self-starting permanent-magnet synchronous motor is essentially a new form of motor with a wide variety of applications

articleTitle: EEV invests in engineering skill and product expertise
abstract: Despite the advent of bigger and better solid-state devices, the market for electronic valves and tubes is still significant and, indeed, is showing some signs of gradual expansion. Many companies, however, which made a reasonable business of selling tubes a few years ago have been forced out of the market place by very hard economic pressures. But the English Electric Valve Company Limited not only has survived but also has been increasing its market share in the field of professional electron tubes. One of the reasons for this, according to ROBERT COULSON, Managing Director of EEV, is that his company believes in recruiting the best engineers, motivating them correctly, and giving them, as far as possible, the best and most up-to-date equipment with which to work in developing new ideas and products. JOHN COOPER, Editor of Electronics & Power, visited EEV's headquarters at Chelmsford, Essex, recently and spoke to Mr. Coulson about his company and about his own ideas on management and the best use of resources, both human and material, in Britain's industry

articleTitle: Emi scanner helps ICR give high-precision radiotherapy
Experimenters prepare for tests with the first Orbital Test Satellite
abstract: The attempt to place the first Orbital Test Satellite (O.T.S.) into geostationary orbit last September ended just 55 s after liftoff when the American Thor-Delta launcher exploded, depositing the satellite in the Atlantic Ocean. A second satellite, constructed by the same European consortium, under the prime contractorship of British Aerospace Dynamics, Stevenage, was successfully launched on the 11th May. This launch marks the culmination of eight years of industrial studies and development with the object of producing a test satellite that could be the forerunner of a European regional communication-satellite system for the 1980s. This system would be primarily used for intra-European telephony circuits and for Eurovision television distribution

articleTitle: Robots in industry - too few or too many?
abstract: Robots are misunderstood by a very large section of the population. The science fiction fan sees Daleks, Star Wars characters or the obedient robots of Isaac Asimov's Invention. The housewife may imagine a robot housekeeper and cleaner; the factory worker may envisage a lost job. Even managers may expect too much of the robot system they plan to install or allow too little for the attitudes of the men and women who have to work among them

In particular, the firm's response to different situations will be described. We are asking you to be involved-to analyse the situation and propose action which you believe the firm should have taken based on your experience. A selection of responses will be printed in a future edition. Remember, a case study only presents a situation, it does not suggest that methods adopted are correct or incorrect. Its use is to promote discussion (in our situation through the medium of Electronics & Power) and through discussion we may learn. In the space allocated it is impossible todescribe the full extent of the situation. It is up to the reader to fill in the gaps and make appropriate assumptions. If you feel you have something to offer, please respond to David Overton at theaddress shown below

Do we as young engineers expect better recognition of the contributions of engineering to society? If so, how can we as individuals, or collectively as members of engineering societies, persuade society to give us this recognition? And lastly, how can the engineering societies help their younger members in their education, training and development as professional engineers?

articleTitle: Programmable controllers. The new revolution in industrial control
abstract: Because of the soaring costs and lack of flexibility experienced when using hard-wired relay or solid-state systems, control engineers have been turning to programmable controllers to solve their problems. But what are the advantages of programmable controllers, their terminology, their present and future technology, and what different programming techniques are available?

articleTitle: Improved electrical safety using a new 13 A e.l.c.b.
Reliability. An aid to design in pursuit of total quality control
abstract: The scope for saving money by implementing a sensible reliability programme is potentially very great, and the money saved should more than cover the cost of the programme. But saving money is not the only benefit: the customer satisfaction you generate should make money

articleTitle: Novel traction system for railway applications
abstract: Traction systems employing the simple and rugged a.c. induction motor have long been the dream of railway engineers. Variable-frequency solid-state inverters have made that dream a reality, and many railway authorities and manufacturers around the world are developing such systems using conventional polyphase induction motors driving the wheels through gears. The Research & Development Division of British Rail has succeeded in building an induction motor entirely within a tubular axle and driving the wheels directly, and so the problems of mounting the motor and its gears which arise with conventional arrangements are eliminated

articleTitle: Instruments in the care of the critically Ill
abstract: Most of us like to steer clear of hospitals (at least as patients), and the intensive-care unit perhaps even more so. However, electronics engineers at least may find themselves at home in this environment. Just as electronic equipment today has a role in almost every other aspect of our lives, in intensive care it is helping to keep alive the critically ill

In 1977 the American journal Byte, a well produced glossy aimed specifically at the amateur computer enthusiast, conducted a survey of its readership with most interesting results. First was the staggering figure of over 100 000 circulation. Secondly, from a random sample of 2163 readers, 35% owned their own computer, which, with a crude estimate, implies around 50 000 installed systems by now. In the UK, growth has been less spectacular, but companies such as Computer Workshop, Computer, Comart, Haywood etc. are importing both complete systems and kits. Computer Workshop and Sintel are now manufacturing in the UK, and there are numerous other `minimum' systems appearing. There is, however, an intriguing side effect for the professional engineer. These systems can be of industrial quality, and systems backed up by floppy discs make cost-effective program development systems. There is also a good range of interfaces available, so that they can well be used in process control applications

This lecture was given by Balth. van der Pol on the 8th December 1938, on his acceptance of the Chair of Electrical Engineering with the Delft Institute. The lecture was printed for local distribution by Martinus Nijhoff, The Hague, in 1938, and this translation is from that edition. The lecture has been edited to about four-fifths its original length

articleTitle: Britain - a world force in semiconductors?
abstract: inMOS is IANN BARRON's second new-venture electronics company. He started Computer Technology Ltd. in the middle 1960s, but he failed to gain the necessary Government backing for this first British minicomputer venture. Can inMOS now succeed? Iann Barron explains his views to DENNIS MORALEE

X-ray computed tomography, derived from the Greek meaning 'to write a slice or section', has been commercially available from 1972, after its invention and development by G.N. Hounsfield at the central research laboratories of EMI in 1967. Since then, its impact on the medical world has been as great as the discovery of X-rays itself, and despite the inherent high cost of the equipment there are already over 1000 systems in hospitals around the world.

articleTitle: Speech output systems and the Captain Kirk problem
abstract: The Captain Kirk problem of a computer-based information system that can be freely accessed by voice and will provide unrestricted spoken output is someway off. This is particularly true of the speech input side. However, at the output level, work is well advanced on the production of high-quality synthetic speech. The intermediate level of input request understanding and generation of output information for speech is a fascinating area, combining methods from artificial intelligence, linguistics and computer science, and much can be expected from a combined application of these disciplines

This article is for the beer drinkers among you microcomputer engineers. It is about the application of the concept of decentralised control, using microcomputers, to calculate and control water and beer flows etc. in the brewing process

A threat to progress, American war games, the well being of Europe: the arguments for and against using nuclear energy ranged back and forth in the open discussions organised by the European Commission in Brussels recently. For three days an invited audience, which included many journalists from all over W. Europe, heard speakers arguing the case for pursuing or for rejecting the nuclear power option. The speakers, invited by the Commission, came from most nuclear nations of the European Community and from outside it. No answers emerged from the discussions, but some interesting questions were asked

In February 1971, the European Organisation for Nuclear Research's member countries signed an agreement to build a 300 GeV accelerator and a new experimental area at a cost not exceeding SF1150 million (1970 values). The accelerator first operated in May 1976 and the new North Experimental Area will be in use by spring this year. The project will be completed well within the budget - SF50 million has already been returned to member states.

Change and expansion have been the predominant features of the electronic components industry in the past 10 years, and component suppliers have multiplied and changed as much as the components they sell. Even as little as six years ago, manufacturers were willing to sell small quantities of their components, and most customers preferred to purchase from the original suppliers. Today the picture has almost reversed; distributors have become the mainstay of component supply to all except the highest volume users of components.

`Cybernetics' has become a vogue word, and it is no longer surprising to hear of cybernetically designed tractor cabs or cybernetically controlled icecream production. Legitimate as all this may well be, one cannot help being suspicious. Despite its popularity, the subject is not really well understood. Some think that it is about brains, robots and machine intelligence. Others connect it in some vague way with engineering and biology. So what is cybernetics? The study of artifical intelligence does fall under the umbrella of cybernetics, but I don't intend to give this aspect much coverage. I think that cybernetics is much more general.

The subject of insulator testing is continuously developing. Tests which are standardised in the publications of the IEC and BSI are the result of careful consideration by experts from manufacturers and users, as well as extensive testing to establish their validity. Although every new test adds to the problems of the designer and manufacturer, the product has an additional guaranteed characteristic

articleTitle: It's back to school for electronics engineers
abstract: The announcement of the electronics industry's latest invention, a programmable large-scale logic circuit known as the microprocessor, was accompanied with as much fanfare as a film star's baby, but it is only now that products incorporating microprocessors are becoming numerous. One of the causes for delay was the considerable initial effort needed from engineers and their managers to understand the microprocessor's advantaaes and limitations. Early users had to teach themselves; but what was really needed was a choice of training programmes, which have only recently become available

articleTitle: A review of the state of the integration art
abstract: Eight years ago Carl den Brinker was asked to present his views on the future of electronics in Electronics & Power. Eight years is a long time, particularly in the semiconductor industry: in 1970 Carl den Brinker predicted that ` ... whole processors will be made in l.s.i.'. The microprocessor has been with us for some time now, but what is next?

Included in the role of the professional electrical engineer is the need continuously to survey the future needs of professional electrical engineers and others, to ensure that the students of today are able to play the fullest part of which they are capable in the years ahead.

articleTitle: Vehicle instrument displays. The electronic revolution
abstract: The car market is acknowledged to be one of the most difficult for electronic systems to penetrate. The combined environment of temperature, humidity, vibration, electrical transients etc., coupled with the required visual appeal and cost targets, are very demanding. Nevertheless, the present state of the available technologies indicates that displays will be available for vehicles in the early 1980s

abstract: Britain's Airborne Early Warning Nimrod programme will cost about £300 million, a cost that it will bear alone as there is little chance of the other NATO countries joining the project. But it is hoped that the project, with Britain's partnership in the Tornado, will keep the country in step with today's military aircraft and radar technologies and allow it to carry out its maritime commitments and assure air defence

articleTitle: Developing crosslinked polyethylene cables for high-voltage power transmission
abstract: 30 years ago, cable engineers dreamed of using polyethylene cables for transmission voltages. Today significant progress is being made in bringing the dream to reality, and the use of polyethylene cables is bound to increase at the lower end of the range

articleTitle: Sparks from steam. The story of the Armstrong hydroelectric generator
abstract: The mysterious explosion of three large oil tankers in 1969 would not appear to have any connection with the pecullar happenings in an isolated Northumberland Colliery in 1840. However, there might have been no explosions had the dangers of the electrification of wet steam and high-pressure water been better appreciated by those responsible for the cleaning out of large oil tanks

The increasing complexity of military electronics systems, coupled with the shortage of skilled technicians, has forced military authorities throughout the world to take a fresh look at maintenance. A careful study is being undertaken of 'whole-life costing', which includes thetotal cost of ownership and maintenance over the equipment's lifetime, and so automatic test equipment is being used in increasing numbers

All people in specialised fields believe that their subjects are wide in their ramifications, and usually there is some truth in it. Hearing protection embraces some knowledge of acoustics, sound-level measurements, anatomy and physiology of the ear, work done in relation to damage caused by noise, various methods of decreasing noise at source and, if this is not possible, hearing protection. The subject can be further extended to a discussion on the need for, and methods of, hearing testing, for workers exposed to hazardous noise

articleTitle: Mil spec computers. Building the hardware to fit the software
abstract: Computers are now an essential part of practically every military system; the US Department of Defence alone spends some $6 billion/year on computing projects. Severe problems have, however, been encountered in the production of reliable software for many defence applications, particularly those using `embedded' computers built into weapons and communication equipment. To overcome these problems, the US military is pursuing an adventurous programme of standardisation that will ultimately allow the use of only one programming language and one machine architecture

For the first 50 years or so after the Wright brothers conclusively demonstrated that heavier than air flight was a feasible and controllable activity, aeroplanes were equipped with relatively simple sets of instruments and electronic devices. This relative simplicity was true of both civil and military aircraft, and included the devices fitted as aids to navigation, for the control of aircraft systems and the displays connected with them, and the operation of weapons systems where appropriate. However, in recent years, aircraft have become integrated systems rather than vehicles that happen to carry a number of disconnected mechanical and electronic devices. One of the best examples of system integration is the navigation/attack (Navattack) system of a modern military aircraft

Good Standards are essential for economic progress - bad standards lead to stagnation of design and uneconomic design; a difficult and delicate balance exists which necessitates clear thinking and real understanding. Britain's Standards should compete worldwide; preferably they should lead, which is one of the best ways of making our technical presence felt, as has been proved on many occasions

articleTitle: Radar to the planets and back
abstract: Generally, we think of radar as a technique widely used for the detection and location of man-made objects like aircraft, ships and speeding cars. Much less often do we consider the use of radar as a tool for exploring the Earth's upper atmosphere and extraterrestrial members of the solar system. But in fact it was in the ionospheric-sounding experiments carried out just over 50 years ago that radar as we now know it has its origins

Whether Charles Cros or Thomas Edison is regarded as the true originator of sound recording and reproduction, 1977 must be acknowledged as the centenary year. It was in 1877 that Cros deposited his proposal with the French Academy of Sciences and, in the same year, Edison was granted US patent 200251 for his phonograph. What a vast industry has sprung from these beginnings! The modern record or `Phonogram', to give it its legal title, is in truth a child of electronics, and the majority of the sophiscated methods now used in its production have evolved in the last 15 years or so in parallel with developments in semiconductor technology

articleTitle: Finance for industry. Part 2: The public company
abstract: In the first article of this series, we examined the financing of the private company, and evaluated a number of the alternative options when raising outside capital with which to buttress the company's own capital production from retained profit. articleTitle: UK's flexible transmission system proves its worth
abstract: Much attention has been paid to the power generation side of the Central Electricity Generating Board's activity, particularly to the controversy surrounding the Drax `B' order and its plant suppliers. articleTitle: The role of avionics in modern aircraft
abstract: Avionics as a term was introduced in the USA in the early 1950s to describe the systems which depend on and exploit electronic technology in the aviation field. Its role has become more and more important in modern aircraft, and the cost of the avionic system now fitted can equal as much as one-third or more of the total aircraft cost. The world market for avionics equipment over the next 10 years is estimated to be in the region of £30 billion, and so its importance for the future can be appreciated

articleTitle: Finance for industry. Part 1: The private company
abstract: This first article in a three-part series discusses the most difficult business of all: getting the money to get your company off the ground. articleTitle: Developing an electronic local exchange register translator for the British Post Office
abstract: The local exchange translator, a telephone exchange subsystem that makes possible the unified telephone numbering schemes of large cities, has existed in its present electromechanical form for some 50 years. Now an electronic replacement has been developed by engineers from Pye TMC Ltd. that makes extensive use of large-scale integration and greatly extends the scope of the electromechanical director equipment

articleTitle: The early days of British computers ߞ 1
abstract: The emergence of a British computer industry is traced during the decade 1945-55 in this two-part article. Part one deals with the immediate post Second World War years, including the 'British national computer' the Cambridge EDSAC and the Manchester Mark 1 and 2. Part 2 will deal with the NPL ACE, MOSAIC, TREAC etc. and concurrent US developments

articleTitle: Satellites. Their impact on world communication
abstract: It is only 20 years since the US Score satellite carried the first communication payload into orbit, and only 13 years since Early Bird inaugurated the first commercial satellite service. Now a 2nd generation of satellites is about to come into commercial use, and an eventual 3rd generation is beginning to be developed. These new satellites will have a considerable effect on communication services, bringing satellite communication directly into everyday life

articleTitle: The effects of climate on energy policy
abstract: Local effects of energy-conversion systems have already been observed, and the influence of cities can already be quantified. The global climate system is, however, a complex nonlinear system, and the large number of feedback loops between its different components mean that it is sensitive to large-scale changes in any one part

abstract: Last month saw the largest change ever in patents laws affecting British industry. articleTitle: Provision of transmitting aerials at the main u.h.f. television stations in the UK
abstract: When the Government authorised the BBC to start a 625-line u.h.f. television service, its engineers were faced with a large design, assessment and commissioning task. articleTitle: Semiconductor technology and the changing world of computing
abstract: The rapid development of the microprocessor has overshadowed developments in minicomputer and mainframe computer technology, and some commentators have forecast the eclipse of these older types of computer. However, significant developments are taking place in mini and mainframe computers, and an analysis of the needs of the three fundamental approaches to the use of computers suggests that there will always be a need for the three very different types of computer.

Public concern about nuclear waste is an important factor in determining how rapidly our nuclear generating capacity can be expanded. It is therefore important that those who advocate expansion of our nuclear programme should understand the real problems of nuclear waste; how it is handled now; how it will be disposed of in the future; and why it will not be the problem suggested by the antinuclear lobby.

articleTitle: Designing reliable computer systems. The fault-tolerant approach - 1
abstract: There are two strategies for increasing the reliability of a computer system. The first, called fault avoidance, is to try and remove the source of every possible fault that could give rise to an error condition. In practice this is not possible and the second strategy, called fault tolerance, is to incorporate various forms of protective redundancy in the form of additional hardware, additional software and time replication. This first part of a two-part tutorial guide to the fault-tolerant approach is a general survey of the many techniques for improving fault tolerance, and comments also on the design of self-checking logic circuits. The second part will look in some detail at one particular implementation (the JPL-Star computer) and concludes with a brief survey of other proposals and implementations

articleTitle: Role of the university electrical engineering department in road traffic studies
abstract: What role can a university electrical-engineering department have in the field of urban-traffic studies? Two principal contributions have been identified. The first comprises a furtherance of fundamental knowledge of traffic behaviour and control achieved through theoretical studies and more particularly via simulation. The second contribution is through the provision of specific projects of limited scope. These typically relate to high-level technology such as might be involved through the use of microprocessors
